introduction: “This is the essence of unity—that ye should behold the True One alone as all-prevailing over all things and manifest in the mirrors of all created things.” Tawḥíd, the affirmation that God is one, is the centre of Islam, and these readings show what Bahá’u’lláh, the Báb and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá make of it. God is one in essence, attributes and acts, beyond number and name. All things are His signs, yet a sign is not a part, and the doctrine that everything is God is set aside. The Manifestations are one in reality, as one sun in many mirrors, and to distinguish among them is to deny unity; the Trinity is explained in those terms. The confession “no God but God” is read as a discipline of negation and affirmation. And unity professed by the tongue alone is worthless: it must become self-surrender and, in the last readings, love and concord among people. The Qur’án and the Hebrew prophets furnish most of the parallels, the Gospel of John the sayings on oneness and station, and the Rig Veda, Xenophanes, Kabír and Ibn ‘Arabí show how widely the One has been confessed. Whitman, Emerson, Spinoza and Pope stand for the unity of existence the readings decline; Feuerbach asks whether every divine name is only a human one.
questions: “Manifest in the mirrors of all created things.” What is the difference between saying that everything is a sign of God and saying that everything is God? Why do the readings care?
Jesus says “I and my Father are one” and also that the Son does not know the hour. How does the idea of “differences of station” read the two sayings?
“Ye must negate negation and then affirm affirmation.” What has to be denied in your own picture of God before the affirmation means anything?
“How many there are who glorify and unify Him … yet are” deprived. James says the devils also believe God is one. What turns the belief into unity?
The Qur’án says “say not Three”; the Creed says “Light of Light.” After reading ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s answer, what could a Christian and a Muslim each recognize in it?
The last readings pass from the oneness of God to “spiritual unity” among friends. Malachi argues the same way. Why should the first lead to the second?

outside.why: “The essence of unity”: to see the True One “manifest in the mirrors of all created things … all things to be sustained by Him.” Paul at Athens: in him we live, and move, and have our being.
The Qur’án says as much of every direction a person can face: whithersoever ye turn, there is Allah’s Countenance.
Hopkins: the world is charged with the grandeur of God. It will flame out, like shining from shook foil.
“How can I not praise Thee when my heart findeth no rest except in Thy remembrance?” The psalm: great is the Lord, and greatly to be praised; and his greatness is unsearchable.
Declare His oneness “with your inner and outer tongues,” so that it shows in what you do. Jesus: not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, but he that doeth the will of my Father.
Israel’s confession of unity passes at once into a way of living: the Lord our God is one Lord: and thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thine heart.
“Is not the magic word oneness synonymous with unity and peace?” John: he that loveth not knoweth not God; for God is love.
“One in His Essence, one in His attributes, one in His works.” The Qur’án: He is Allah, the One! And there is none comparable unto Him.

Some talk of stations of unity that erase the difference between Creator and creature, and Bahá’u’lláh says it leads to “idleness and vain imaginings.” Whitman speaks for that confidence: divine am I inside and out, and I make holy whatever I touch. What is lost when the distinction of stations goes?

Emerson in the woods: all mean egotism vanishes; I am part or parcel of God. Is this the experience the reading warns against, or a report of what the first reading calls seeing God “manifest in the mirrors of all created things”?
‘Abdu’l-Bahá is asked about the Trinity and its three Persons. The doctrine as the Creed states it: one Lord Jesus Christ, God of God, Light of Light, of one substance with the Father.
The Qur’án’s reply to it: say not “Three”—Cease! it is better for you!—Allah is only One. How does ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s explanation by the sun and the mirror do justice to both?
“He hath none to equal Him in the whole universe.” Paul: there is none other God but one.
The divine reality is manifest in the Prophets “as the sun becomes resplendent in various mirrors.” Paul: who is the image of the invisible God.
Jesus to Philip: he that hath seen me hath seen the Father.
Differences of utterance come from “differences of station.” From the station of oneness: I and my Father are one.
And from the station of servitude, in the same Gospels: of that day and that hour knoweth no man, neither the Son, but the Father.
The Manifestations speak as one who has always been. Jesus: before Abraham was, I am.
They “resemble the sun which no matter how often it riseth and setteth is still the one and the same sun.” Krishna: I rise, from age to age, and take visible shape.
“Beware … lest ye be tempted to make any distinction between any of the Manifestations.” The Qur’án: we make no distinction between any of His messengers.

By the “Unity of God” is meant that the Founders of the religions “are to be regarded as one soul.” The Qur’án’s creed: we believe in that which was revealed unto Abraham, and Moses and Jesus received; we make no distinction between any of them.
Each stands in the station of the one before. Jesus: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil.
Created through His Word and most distinguished among the people. Hebrews: God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets.
One sun, two effects. The reading quotes the Qur’án: a healing and a mercy for believers though it increase the evil-doers in naught save ruin.
“The Truth hath ever been, and will ever be.” The psalm: from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God.
The wonders of His oneness “have ever existed through Thy creation.” Paul: the invisible things of him are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made.

To say all things are signs of God does not mean that God is all things or that all are equal. Spinoza drew the conclusion the reading refuses: all things which are, are in God. What does the reading protect by refusing it?
Pope: all are but parts of one stupendous whole, whose body nature is and God the soul. Why is a sign not a part?
The signs differ in degree. Paul: there is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon; one star differeth from another star in glory.
Wordsworth keeps to the language of sign and presence: a sense sublime of something far more deeply interfused, a motion and a spirit that rolls through all things.
From “unity of existence” to seeing the One in all. Blake: to see a World in a Grain of Sand and a Heaven in a Wild Flower.
In the valley of unity the wayfarer “gazeth upon the manifestations of singleness.” Kabír: from the One Light, the entire universe welled up. So, who is good, and who is bad?
Ibn ‘Arabí: my heart has become capable of every form; I follow the religion of Love.
“There is no Lord but the Exalted One.” Isaiah: look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth: for I am God, and there is none else.
“All things have borne witness to Thy oneness.” The psalm: the heavens declare the glory of God.
Job: ask now the beasts, and they shall teach thee; speak to the earth, and it shall teach thee.
“Whenever I have sought other than Thee, I found it naught.” The psalmist: whom have I in heaven but thee?
From the highest heights to the lowest depths, He is found. The psalm: if I ascend up into heaven, thou art there: if I make my bed in hell, behold, thou art there.
No speck of dust but tells of His wisdom. Whitman: a leaf of grass is no less than the journey-work of the stars.
“The atoms have spoken.” The Qur’án: there is not a thing but hymneth His praise; but ye understand not their praise.
Jesus: if these should hold their peace, the stones would immediately cry out.
God sanctified the world through the word “No” and guided it to the city of “Except.” The sentence being read: know that there is no God save Allah.
Isaiah’s form of it also denies before it affirms: beside me there is no God.
“Through the word ‘no’ [He] caused all the manifestations of negation to perish.” The first commandment begins with the same word: thou shalt have no other gods before me.
“Ye must negate negation and then affirm affirmation.” The Tao Te Ching begins by taking names away: the name that can be named is not the enduring and unchanging name.
“That the word might be fulfilled that He is the First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden.” The word, from the Qur’án: He is the First and the Last, and the Outward and the Inward.
John heard it too: I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the ending.
Every letter of the sacred words has an inner and an outer aspect. Aquinas: it is not unfitting if, even according to the literal sense, one word in Holy Writ should have several senses.
God is the One, and all else zeros that have value only with the One before them. Jesus: without me ye can do nothing.

The philosophers also began from the One. Plotinus: seeking nothing, possessing nothing, lacking nothing, the One is perfect and has overflowed. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s arithmetic makes the same point for a general audience. What does his image add about the worth of the “zeros”?
“Most men, in the plane of reality, behold not the Real.” Plato’s prisoners: to them the truth would be literally nothing but the shadows of the images.
Unify thy Lord “through negating names and attributes.” Pascal: having neither parts nor limits, He has no affinity to us. We are then incapable of knowing either what He is or if He is.
Wittgenstein ends where the Báb begins: whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent. The Báb does not fall silent; he negates, and then worships. What is the difference?

“Flee unto His presence from the mention of anything other than His Essence in the station of His worship.” Jesus, refusing a rival: thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve.
The prayer every Muslim repeats: Thee alone we worship; Thee alone we ask for help.
“All are from God and unto Him shall all return.” The Qur’án: Lo! we are Allah’s and lo! unto Him we are returning.
Paul: of him, and through him, and to him, are all things.
A testimony made on a day of fasting. The Levites on Israel’s day of fasting: thou, even thou, art Lord alone; thou hast made heaven, the heaven of heavens, with all their host.
One melody of thy Lord “would enrapture all the worlds.” The psalm: deep calleth unto deep.
“I shall glorify Thee, praise Thee, proclaim Thy unity, magnify Thee.” The last verse of the Psalter: let every thing that hath breath praise the Lord.
“There is no God but Thee, as Thou hast testified to Thine own Self.” The Qur’án: Allah Himself is Witness that there is no God save Him.
“There is no God but Him, alone with no partner.” Moses: the Lord he is God; there is none else beside him.
The oldest hymns of India: to what is One, sages give many a title.
And among the Greeks, Xenophanes: one god, the greatest among gods and men.

“How many there are who glorify and unify Him throughout all days and nights, yet are among the most” deprived. James: thou believest that there is one God; thou doest well: the devils also believe, and tremble.
Isaiah: this people draw near me with their mouth, and with their lips do honour me, but have removed their heart far from me.

“The oneness of God … is not” a matter of words. A scribe agreed with Jesus that God is one and that to love Him is more than all burnt offerings, and was told: thou art not far from the kingdom of God.
Whoever beholds Him “as the One dominating, prevailing over, and encompassing all things” is of the people of unity. The psalm: our God is in the heavens: he hath done whatsoever he hath pleased.
Whoever ascribes partnership “is deprived of the light of true divine unity.” The Qur’án: Allah forgiveth not that a partner should be ascribed unto Him.
“Cast aside vain imaginings … idols and their likes.” The psalm: they have mouths, but they speak not: eyes have they, but they see not.

Feuerbach turned the attack on idols against belief in God itself: the true sense of Theology is Anthropology; there is no distinction between the predicates of the divine and human nature. How do the readings’ own negations (“sanctified from all names”) meet him?
A word that distinguishes “between the ungodly and the believers.” Elijah on Carmel: if the Lord be God, follow him: but if Baal, then follow him.
Those who “broke the covenant and pledge of the idols.” Paul: ye turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God.
A day wherein “grace hath encompassed all religions.” Zechariah: in that day shall there be one Lord, and his name one.
“Is there doubt about God?” The question is from the Qur’án: can there be doubt concerning Allah, the Creator of the heavens and the earth?
“The effulgences of the Light of Manifestation have illumined the world.” Isaiah: the Gentiles shall come to thy light, and kings to the brightness of thy rising.
Verses that “call the people to the recognition of His Self.” Isaiah: I am God, and there is none else; I am God, and there is none like me.
The Sun shines, “yet most turn away.” John: he came unto his own, and his own received him not.

“By Thine aloneness the Sun of Oneness shone, and by Thy banishment the land of Unity was adorned.” Isaiah’s servant, through whom many are made whole: he is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows.
“The station of absolute self-surrender transcendeth … every other station.” Jesus in the garden: not my will, but thine, be done.
“Consecrate thyself to the Will of God.” A soul in Dante’s Paradise on why none there envies another: to keep itself within the will divine, whereby our very wishes are made one.

He “Who from everlasting hath inhabited the inaccessible heights.” Isaiah: the high and lofty One that inhabiteth eternity; I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also that is of a contrite and humble spirit.
“Thou art He Whose mercy hath preceded all things.” The Name proclaimed on Sinai: The Lord God, merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth.
A prayer by the Name that “didst open the gate of Divine Unity to all servants.” The psalmist’s prayer for sight: open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law.
“How sweet is beholding the signs of Thy oneness.” The psalm: how sweet are thy words unto my taste! yea, sweeter than honey to my mouth!
That they “may acknowledge Thy Oneness.” The psalmist asks for a heart to match it: unite my heart to fear thy name.
“My tongue beareth witness to Thy unity and singleness.” Isaiah: I am the Lord, and there is none else, there is no God beside me.
“You have no partner, no peer, no likeness.” The Qur’án: naught is as His likeness.
“To plunge into the ocean of Thy oneness.” Paul’s prayer: that ye might be filled with all the fulness of God.
Loved ones “who have held fast to the cord of Thy oneness.” The Qur’án: hold fast, all of you together, to the cable of Allah, and do not separate.
Those who testify as God has testified. Paul: one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in you all.
In every age the Sun of Truth “bestows the light of unity” so that limited realities become one. Jesus’s prayer: that they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee.
Malachi argues from the One to the many: have we not all one father? hath not one God created us? why do we deal treacherously every man against his brother?
“The lights of oneness are shining.” Paul at Athens: God hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth.
“The Light of Truth shineth radiantly in the lamp of Divine Unity and in the niche of Oneness.” The images are from the Light Verse: the similitude of His light is as a niche wherein is a lamp.
“Enter beneath the shade of the Word of Unity.” The psalm: behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!
The last hymn of the Rig Veda: assemble, speak together: let your minds be all of one accord.
“The day will soon come when the light of Divine unity will have so permeated the East and the West.” Isaiah: the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea.

God “has bestowed infinite love between the hearts and souls of His friends and established spiritual unity.” The Qur’án: if thou hadst spent all that is in the earth thou couldst not have attuned their hearts, but Allah hath attuned them.
Paul: above all these things put on charity, which is the bond of perfectness.

quran-know-that-there-is-no-god-save-all.text: So know (O Muhammad) that there is no Allah save Allah, and ask forgiveness for thy sin and for believing men and believing women. Allah knoweth (both) your place of turmoil and your place of rest.

quran-can-there-be-doubt-concerning-alla.text: Their messengers said: Can there be doubt concerning Allah, the Creator of the heavens and the earth? He calleth you that He may forgive you your sins and reprieve you unto an appointed term. They said: Ye are but mortals like us, who would fain turn us away from what our fathers used to worship. Then bring some clear warrant.
